paper_title: Beyond Code and Pixels: Co-Generating Editable and Visually Rich Presentations

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Generating PPTX presentations is a structured task that requires semantic planning, visual composition, precise layout, and editability, motivating collaboration among specialized agents. However, programmatic methods offer editability but often produce rigid designs, while image-based methods provide visual richness but flatten content into difficult-to-edit pixels. A hybrid system can combine these strengths, but must coordinate interdependent decisions across content, layout, and appearance. To address this challenge, we propose SlidesWeaver, a hybrid multi-agent system that coordinates language and vision agents through shared deck- and slide-level states. Specifically, it uses staged multimodal commitment, diffusion-based composition planning, and two generation schedules for different priorities between composition freedom and accurate text preservation, while preserving native text and geometry. Across 1,728 generations spanning 24 system-model configurations, SlidesWeaver achieves consistently superior overall quality across all evaluated dimensions while maintaining structural control, editability, and practical generation efficiency.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Presentation generation transforms structured presentation request together with style brief into coherent sequence of slides that communicates narrative through text and visual composition [9, 14, 23]. Accordingly, generated presentation must coordinate semantic content, visual organization, and editable structure, because these components jointly determine what the audience understands and how the deck can be revised. Given different presentation scenarios place different weights on visual expressiveness and editability, meeting such flexible goals therefore requires an intelligent system that coordinates structural control and visual expressiveness throughout the generation process [4, 22]. Existing approaches largely divide into two paradigms with complementary strengths. Programmatic methods construct slides through structured operations or executable representations, such WSDM 27, February 1519, 2027, Hong Kong, China Zhou et al. as editing actions, layout programs, or HTML-like code [6, 10]. Recent agentic systems organize this structured generation process across specialized roles for research, planning, and design [13, 16, 23, 24]. While available, image generation often serves as an optional action for acquiring visual material alongside web retrieval, leaving the core composition process to the structured authoring agents. These explicit representations provide precise control over text and geometry, yet their structural primitives tend to produce rigid or repetitive compositions with limited visual expressiveness [6, 20]. Conversely, image-centric methods draw on generative visual priors to create richer illustrations, styles, and compositions [20]. However, rasterization flattens text, geometry, and their relationships into pixels, making individual elements difficult to edit or recover reliably [1, 11, 25]. Thus, current systems typically gain either structural control or visual freedom at the expense of the other. Combining these paradigms within multi-agent system introduces coordination problem, which is that specialized agents make interdependent decisions through different representations. Content, composition, and geometry constrain one another: text length determines the space required by layout, visual composition determines how that text is grouped and perceived, and the available geometry determines how much content can be expressed clearly. Premature commitment by any agent propagates constraints downstream. Fixed geometry limits subsequent visual exploration, while in contrast, complete raster rendering removes the structure required for precise editing [1, 6]. The central question is therefore which agent should commit content, composition, geometry, and visual appearance, and when? We formulate presentation generation as staged multimodal commitment, coordination principle through which agents progressively commit these decisions as their constraints become available. Based on this formulation, we introduce SlidesWeaver, hybrid multi-agent system that coordinates language and vision agents through shared deckand slide-level states. deck-level director establishes the narrative and visual language; for each slide, specialized agents use low-step diffusion model to explore compositions, ground selected proposal into explicit text and visual regions, synthesize geometry-registered visual elements, and critique the rendered result. This design places generative visual models inside both the planning and synthesis loops while retaining the structured state required for editable assembly. Within this mechanism, SlidesWeaver supports two commitment schedules that prioritize different relationships between composition and text. Figure 1 shows representative outputs from both schedules across four distinct visual styles. ❶ Layout-conditioned text generation grounds diffusion proposal before generating copy according to the resulting regions and capacities, allowing composition to shape the final wording. ❷ Text-constrained layout generation commits the generated text first and then grounds the diffusion proposal around that exact copy, favoring scenarios where preserving accurate, pre-committed text is stronger requirement. Both schedules yield the same structured PPTX representation with native text, explicit geometry, and separate control of raster elements. Because both schedules produce the same structured PPTX representation, we evaluate SlidesWeaver on 72 cases spanning six domains and two complementary input tracks. We compare it with three academic systems using visual expressiveness, instruction following, content quality, layout validity, topological diversity, cost, latency, and first-pass success as evaluation criteria. Across 15 language-modelmetric comparisons, one of our two routes achieves every best quality score, while the Text First route improves over the strongest baseline by 14.2% in visual expressiveness, 15.9% in instruction following, 17.7% in content quality, 20.3% in layout validity, and 22.9% in topological diversity. The slide-separable architecture also supports parallel execution and bounded visualsynthesis budgets: Topology First costs 37.3% less and runs 57.7% faster than the image-enabled DeepPresenter baseline, and six of the eight non-dominated configurations on the quality-cost-latency frontier belong to SlidesWeaver. Our ablations support the mechanism behind these gains: removing diffusion lowers the average Topo-Vendi score from 0.84 to 0.54, while removing the layout judge lowers average Layout from 0.95 to 0.85. Pixel-space exploration, structured grounding, and staged multi-agent coordination thus offer complementary benefits for editable presentation generation. We summarize our contributions as follows: We propose SlidesWeaver, hybrid multi-agent framework for editable presentation generation with two complementary routes: Topology First for layout-conditioned text generation and Text First for text-constrained layout generation. We integrate pixel-space diffusion into the PPTX pipeline to propose slide topologies and synthesize geometry-registered visual elements, enabling visually rich and topologically diverse slides with native text and editable geometry. We design deckand slide-level multi-agent coordination that uses shared context, parallel execution, style reuse, and consolidated synthesis and achieves superior performance and strong trade-offs among quality, cost, and latency.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Figure 2: Comparison of three presentation-generation paradigms. Programmatic methods preserve editability but offer limited visual creativity, while image-centric generation improves aesthetics at the cost of text fidelity and editability. SlidesWeaver combines both strengths, producing visually rich, granularly editable slides with an optimized cost-latency profile. Beyond Code and Pixels: Co-Generating Editable and Visually Rich Presentations WSDM 27, February 1519, 2027, Hong Kong, China Figure 3: Overview of SlidesWeaver, multi-agent system for hybrid PPTX generation. shared Input & Deck Planning Phase establishes deck-level semantic, narrative, and visual context. During Deck Generation, specialized agents follow two complementary routes: Topology First grounds diffusion-proposed structure and adapts text to it, while Text First preserves intended content and uses diffusion to guide and validate executable geometry. Finally, the Visual Synthesis and Assembly Agents convert structured slide states into coherent visual layers and editable PPTX slides. Programmatic Presentation Generation. Early document-toslide systems formulate presentation generation as structured prediction: Doc2PPT summarizes source documents, retrieves text and figures, and predicts their slide layouts [9]. Recent systems replace task-specific predictors with executable representations [7, 18, 19]. AutoPresent generates visual programs through high-level slide API [10], while PPTAgent preserves reference designs by producing executable editing actions [23]. Subsequent work expands the design and revision process [15]: DeepSlides separates page design from code implementation [6], and DeepPresenter organizes generation into researcherpresenter pipeline in which one agent prepares manuscript and assets, another authors HTML slides, and rendered artifacts provide feedback for revision [24]. This progression improves planning flexibility and robustness while retaining explicit, editable structure, but the final composition remains encoded through executable primitives. Image-Centric and Editable Visual Generation. Image-centric generation moves composition into pixel space and avoids restricting every visual element to predefined slide primitive. Current state-of-the-art image models include GPT Image 2 and Nano Banana Pro [2]. The resulting renderings, however, are static raster artifacts without object separation or text reflow [3, 20]. DrawAI follows top-down reconstruction route that recovers editable artifacts from completed raster images: it first infers authoring structure from flattened pixels and then synthesizes valid, manipulable objects [1]. This post-hoc recovery introduces an additional parsing-and-reconstruction burden because region and text proposals can be incomplete, duplicated, or semantically fragmented [1]. These complementary limitations call for hybrid pipeline that uses image-generation priors for visual exploration while committing text, geometry, and object structure in editable form.

sections.title: 3 Method
sections.content: SlidesWeaver is hybrid visual-rich presentation generation system that combines pixel-space generative priors with structured slide representations. Its design is motivated by fundamental representation mismatch: visual composition is ultimately judged in pixel space, whereas an editable presentation must be realized through explicit topology, geometry, and object structure. We therefore separate composition proposal from structural commitment, using diffusion to propose visual organization and grounding to determine how strongly that proposal constrains the executable slide. Figure 3 provides an overview of the resulting three-stage pipeline and the two complementary generation routes.

sections.title: 3.2 Input & Deck Planning Phase
sections.content: The Input & Deck Planning Phase establishes the deck-level narrative and visual identity before generating individual slides. The Planning Agent organizes the request 𝑞 into narrative 𝑁 and semantic intent 𝑀𝑖 for each slide, while the Styling Agent uses the style instruction 𝑠 to define shared visual language 𝑉 , canonical background 𝐵, and reusable visual resources 𝑅: = (cid:0)𝑁 , {𝑀𝑖 }𝑛 𝑖=1 , 𝑉 , 𝐵, 𝑅(cid:1) . (2) These shared decisions remain deliberately high-level. They constrain the decks narrative and visual identity without prescribing slide-specific composition or geometry. Committing finer-grained layout decisions at this stage would prematurely constrain the downstream search space and reduce the room for slide-specific visual exploration. Each slide therefore retains the flexibility to determine its own composition, text realization, and geometry in the subsequent generation phase.

sections.title: 3.3 Deck Generation Phase
sections.content: Why pixel-space proposal is needed. Pure code-based geometry planning (e.g. SVG-based and HTML-based) conflates composition discovery with layout execution. In our HTML-only observations, structurally valid plans repeatedly concentrate on small set of regular composition families. The representation-feedback mismatch explains this behavior: balance, hierarchy, negative space, and topology become visible after rendering, while the planner must already commit the decomposition and coordinates that produce them in vast search space. While rendering closes the loop for correction only after the composition has been chosen, the Judge Agent can consequently repair local overflow, overlap, and spacing defects, but replacing the composition with fundamentally different topology requires new proposal. Figure 4 illustrates the effect of pixel-space proposals on fixed five-slide hospital-ransomware brief. Without diffusion proposal, the Composition-Inspired Grounding Agent produces valid but visually conservative topologies, closely resembling the regular layouts generated by DeepPresenter. In contrast, both SlidesWeaver routes explore substantially different relational organizations across the same deck, including dual-track, branching, ownership-centered, and action-triad compositions. This qualitative difference is reflected by the normalized topology Vendi score [8]. While DeepPresenter obtains 0.5423 and the HTML-only ablation drops to 0.5066, Topology First and Text First reach 0.7986 and 0.8042, respectively, showing the effectiveness of pixel-space proposals in discovering diverse relational organizations. Notably, diffusion serves two complementary roles in our framework. Before structural commitment, it acts as pixel-space exploration mechanism, using its generative prior to discover creative compositions beyond predefined regions and layout primitives, including unconventional grouping, asymmetry, negative space, and visual hierarchy. After the slide structure has been determined, diffusion instead acts as visual synthesis mechanism, transforming the committed semantic and geometric structure into visually rich and instructive content. We therefore use lightweight local diffusion for open-ended composition exploration and reserve more capable remote generation for final visual realization. Further discussion related to local diffusion is placed in Appendix C. Topology First: layout-conditioned text. Topology First method applies when the slide semantics are fixed but their exact verbal realization can adapt to the discovered composition for more coherent content delivery. Given the slide-level semantic intent 𝑀𝑖 , the Composition Agent first generates pixel-space proposal 𝑃𝑖 that explores candidate visual organization. Rather than treating its pixel coordinates as exact geometry, the Topology Grounding Agent extracts the underlying relational structure and converts it into an executable topology together with coarse spatial scaffold and regional capacity constraints: (𝑇𝑖, 𝐺𝑖, 𝐾𝑖 ) = Γtopo (𝑃𝑖 ). Considering the inherently shift-prone nature of the diffusion process, we apply the deterministic, slot-aware matting procedure (detailed in Appendix B) to extract generated content within each registered region. The extraction step is what turns pixel-space generation into geometry-conforming, independently placeable asset. After generation, the system extracts the synthesized content within each registered region into separate transparent layer, 𝑎𝑖 𝑗 = extract (cid:16) (cid:101)𝐴𝑖, 𝑔𝑖 𝑗 (cid:17) , 𝑗 V𝑖, (12) and places these layers back at the geometry specified by 𝐺𝑖 . This preserves the spatial organization validated by Composition-Inspired Grounding Agent while turning each generated visual into an independently selectable and editable slide object. Consequently, this geometry-registered construction provides stronger metric control and object-level editability. Constrained assembly and refinement. Both routes finally assemble generated visuals with editable native text into the slide representation. Text, its associated holder, and local decoration are treated as single content unit so that subsequent refinement cannot break their spatial correspondence. Deterministic fitting is applied first to resolve local sizing and overflow, after which the Judge Agent may propose only localized modifications that respect the structure already committed by the corresponding route. Each candidate modification is re-rendered and accepted only when it improves the slide without introducing collision, semantic loss, or violations of the committed topology or geometry. The judge therefore acts as constrained refiner rather than second layout planner. Topology First method preserves the discovered relational organization while allowing limited geometric adaptation to the realized canvas; Text First method preserves the HTML-derived geometric contract throughout synthesis and assembly. Together, the two strategies expose complementary operating points between scene-level visual integration and precise, editable geometric control.

sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: We evaluate SlidesWeaver along three complementary dimensions: overall presentation quality, the contribution of diffusionbased composition planning, and reliability and practical efficiency. Specifically, we investigate the following research questions. RQ1: Overall presentation quality. How do SlidesWeaver and existing presentation generators compare in visual expressiveness, instruction following, content quality, and layout validity? Models and Baselines. We compare SlidesWeaver against three academic presentation generation systems: AutoPresent, which constructs structured visual programs [10]; DeepSlides, which separates slide design from code realization [6]; and DeepPresenter, which adopts an environment-grounded researcherpresenter pipeline [24]. For all methods, we evaluate three text backbones: GPT 5.4, Gemini 3.1 Pro, and Qwen 3.8 Max. For the image-enabled DeepPresenter and SlidesWeaver (Text First and Topology First), each text backbone is paired with either GPT Image 2 or Nano Banana Pro. This results in 3 configurations for each image-free baseline and 6 configurations for each imageenabled system, for 24 configurations in total. Since all evaluated systems produce editable PPTX files, editability is treated as an output requirement rather than comparative quality dimension. Test Set. Following evaluation settings in [23, 24], we construct test set of 72 presentation requests covering six domains including Science, Technology, Business, Education, Society, and Culture / Creative. The test set contains two complementary tracks. The topic-driven track asks systems to develop presentation from given topic, while the goal-oriented track additionally specifies an explicit communication objective. Across both tracks, we consider six common presentation goals: explaining concept, teaching an audience, persuading, comparing alternatives or supporting decision, reporting evidence, and narrating or inspiring. The benchmark is balanced across the two tracks and six domains, with 36 cases per track and 12 cases per domain. The cases also vary in compositional difficulty, including 17 low-, 29 medium-, and 26 highdifficulty requests. Each case specifies the topic, target audience, communication goal, success criterion, style brief, language, and requested number of slides. Evaluation Protocol. We evaluate all 24 model-system configurations on the full 72-case test set, resulting in 1,728 generation cases. We record the generated artifacts, generation events, latency, and failures for every run. For quality evaluation, common blinded judge based on GPT 5.6 Terra receives the original case brief, extracted slide text, artifact-level evidence, and the ordered slide montage. Following established presentation-generation evaluation protocols and recent benchmarks [46, 10, 12, 20, 23], we evaluate each generated deck along the following dimensions: Visual Expressiveness (VE). Measures the slide designs visual richness, composition quality, and effectiveness on 1-5 scale. Instruction Following (IF). Measures how well the generated deck follows the requested topic, audience, communication goal, style brief, and slide-count constraints on 1-5 scale. sections.title: 4.2 Results and Discussion
sections.content: Table 1 summarizes the results over all 72 presentation requests. Each row gives model configuration. For general comparison, we average cost and latency over each systems configurations. RQ1: Overall presentation quality. SlidesWeaver shows clear overall quality advantage. Across the 15 language-model metric comparisons in Table 1, every best score is achieved by one of our two routes. The two routes represent complementary generation strategies: Text First emphasizes faithful realization of pre-committed text and geometry, whereas Topology First allows the visual composition to play stronger role in shaping the final slide. For the text-preservation-oriented Text First route, averaging over its six configurations yields improvements of 14.2% in VE, 15.9% in IF, 17.7% in Content, 20.3% in Layout, and 22.9% in TopoVendi over the strongest baseline for each metric. Together, the two routes enable SlidesWeaver to combine strong content quality and instruction following with expressive and structurally diverse slide designs, rather than excelling in only single quality dimension. The metric-level results further reveal how these gains arise. Visual expressiveness is naturally sensitive to the underlying image backbone. Within SlidesWeaver, GPT Image 2 achieves higher VE than Nano Banana Pro in every matched setting. Importantly, our pipeline consistently translates this stronger image-generation capability into higher presentation-level visual expressiveness, suggesting that SlidesWeaver can effectively exploit improvements in the underlying image model rather than bottlenecking them during slide construction. For instruction following, the advantage is WSDM 27, February 1519, 2027, Hong Kong, China Zhou et al. more structural. The generation process is decomposed into small, well-specified stages, with each agent responsible for focused subtask and explicit topology or geometry providing additional constraints. The two routes then make different commitments within this shared framework. Text First fixes generated text and geometry before visual synthesis, naturally favoring text preservation and stable layout, while Topology First preserves greater freedom for composition-driven generation. The latter thus depends more on the image models spatial controllability; for example, Nano Banana Pro more readily deviates from the prescribed topology, explaining its lower Layout scores in several Topology First settings. RQ2: Topology and layout diversity. Diffusion-based composition planning substantially expands the structural design space. Topology First and Text First achieve average Topo-Vendi scores of 0.845 and 0.840, respectively, compared with 0.683 for the strongest baseline, corresponding to gains of 23.7% and 22.9%. Importantly, this improvement reflects topological rather than merely stylistic diversity: the generated slides vary in grouping, hierarchy, and spatial organization, rather than only in colors or decorative assets. The nearly identical Topo-Vendi scores of the two routes are particularly informative, as they show that the diversity persists under different downstream realization strategies when translating diffusion proposals into precise geometry. This suggests that the shared diffusion proposal itself provides the structural diversity prior, rather than the effect arising from particular commitment mechanism. Moreover, Text First retains Topo-Vendi of 0.840 while achieving an average Layout score of 0.950, demonstrating that the expanded design space can remain compatible with highly valid slide layouts. We further isolate the contribution of diffusion-based composition planning in the ablation study. it 37.3% cheaper and 57.7% faster than DeepPresenter, while Text First delivers the strongest overall quality at $0.88 per deck and 1,279.9 seconds, remaining 13.7% cheaper and 2.9% faster. Consequently, six of the eight non-dominated configurations in Figure 5 belong to SlidesWeaver, pushing the quality-cost-latency frontier beyond existing systems. This is particularly notable because SlidesWeaver performs more involved visual synthesis than DeepPresenter, which incorporates images through text-only image tool calls. Our pipeline additionally requires mask-conditioned generation and subsequent asset extraction to preserve planned geometry and editability. Despite additional input tokens, SlidesWeaver remains cheaper and faster end-to-end. The system is also highly reliable, with first-pass success rates of 97.69% for Topology First and 96.99% for Text First, demonstrating that the proposed hybrid generation paradigm is efficient and robust in practical use.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We presented SlidesWeaver, hybrid multi-agent system that combines diffusion-based pixel-space exploration with structured presentation slides construction through staged multimodal commitment. Across 72 diverse cases, its two generation routes deliver leading visual, semantic, layout, and topological quality while preserving editable text and geometry. The slide-separable design further supports practical parallel execution with favorable cost and latency, providing strong foundation for efficient, visually rich, and editable presentation generation. The availability of both tool types, however, does not by itself constitute pipeline-level hybrid generation. In this work, we use hybrid specifically to denote the integration of visual generation into composition planning and structured slide realization, rather than its optional use as source of raster assets. To characterize how visual generation is used under this distinction, we probe DeepPresenter on ten randomly selected evaluation cases with three consistent language-model backbones in Table 1, exposing both image search and generation in every run. We use local stubs that preserve tool interfaces and record action traces without invoking remote visual APIs, thereby avoiding differences in retrieved or generated artifact quality from influencing tool-selection behavior. Across all 30 runs, only two action patterns occur: search download generation in 23 runs and search generation in the remaining 7. No run invokes generation before search or interleaves search and generation, and all 117 image-generation events occur after the final search_images action of the corresponding job. The observed policy therefore consistently follows search-first, generation-later sequence, treating generation as subsequent visual-asset acquisition step rather than an initial mechanism for exploring slide composition. In our evaluation presented in Table 1, we disable the image-search API to remove retrieval as competing visual source, thereby giving DeepPresenter maximal opportunity to exploit image generation and enabling fairer comparison of visual-generation capability. This behavior is consistent with the architectural distinction underlying our hybrid-generation claim. In DeepPresenter, searched and generated images are collected as visual assets, while the downstream programmatic pipeline determines slide composition and geometry. In SlidesWeaver, visual generation instead participates on both sides of structural commitment: before commitment, diffusion explores composition and topology in pixel space; after commitment, it synthesizes visually rich and instructive content under the established semantic and geometric structure. Our contribution therefore lies in integrating visual generation throughout composition planning, structured synthesis, and editable assembly, rather than merely exposing image generation as an optional tool within programmatic presentation pipeline. sections.title: D Case Study and Further Discussion
sections.content: We use lightweight local diffusion model, Z-Image-Turbo, to generate one 16:9 pixel-space composition proposal for each slide [21]. The prompt contains only the slide title, coarse communicative purpose, and concise visual logic, while detailed body text and exact coordinates are deliberately omitted to preserve compositional freedom. The resulting raster is used only as visual reference for grounding; readable text, executable geometry, and final visual appearance are determined by subsequent stages. key advantage of this proposal mechanism is its ability to explore diverse compositions with minimal intervention. As illustrated in Figure 7, changing only the random seed produces substantially different organizations for the same slide intent, varying grouping, hierarchy, spatial balance, asymmetry, and use of negative space. This provides the grounding agents with lightweight but expressive proposal space rather than forcing them to construct layouts directly from predefined geometric primitives. The following block provides the complete Slide 01 prompt as our example for the composition-proposal stage. This section presents five fixed-combination qualitative comparisons from the evaluation set. The cases progress from compact didactic brief to increasingly demanding narrative, causal, and dependency-rich briefs. In order, they cover spaced practice, collaborative animation, censusto-funding, multilingual classroom participation, and neighborhood readiness for extreme-weather outages. Each figure compares the same five systemsSlidesWeaver (Topology First), SlidesWeaver (Text First), AutoPresent, DeepSlides, and DeepPresenteron one case. To ensure fair comparison, we fix the language and image backbones across systems. Here, GPT+GPT and Qwen+GPT pair GPT5.4 and Qwen 3.8 Max, respectively, with GPT Image 2; the imagefree baselines use the corresponding text backbone. D.1 Content Density Is Model-Dependent The comparisons expose model-dependent content-density effect. For some briefs, language model expands explanations, adds qualifiers, or enumerates more steps than another model under the Beyond Code and Pixels: Co-Generating Editable and Visually Rich Presentations WSDM 27, February 1519, 2027, Hong Kong, China same slide budget. The additional content can improve coverage, but it also increases the visual workload passed to planning and synthesis, producing denser text blocks and less negative space. This effect is especially visible in cases whose success criterion depends on multi-step explanation, such as the census-to-funding and emergency-readiness cases. The observation motivates treating verbosity as controllable generation variable. Content planning should allocate detail jointly with the topology and the available visual area, instead of assuming that all language backbones produce comparable text volumes. D.2 Inpainting Quality Shapes Topology First

sections.title: Method
sections.content: The second pattern concerns spatial realization. Topology First commits to relational structure before visual synthesis; its inpainting stage must honor registered regions and preserve ownership across neighboring elements. When masks or boundaries are imprecise, foreground content can drift across regions and create overlap even when the topology is coherent. This behavior is consistent with the synthesis ablation in Table 3: layered generation raises Topology First Layout from 0.72 to 0.87 on average, whereas replacing layered generation with inpainting lowers Text First Layout from 0.95 to 0.79. The case studies make the same dependency visible at the artifact level. Topology planning supplies the structure, while image-model spatial controllability determines how faithfully that structure is rendered. As suggested by the results in Table 1, more capable inpainting models provide direct path to better Topology First decks. Improved mask adherence and boundary control would preserve the routes freedom to explore expressive composition while reducing spill and overlap, yielding more elegant and polished editable presentations without changing the planning interface in the future.

sections.title: E Evaluation Prompt and Scoring Procedure
sections.content: We evaluate each generated deck with one blinded visionlanguagemodel (VLM) request. The request contains the frozen presentation brief (topic, audience, communication goal, success criterion, style brief, language, and requested slide count), deterministic generation evidence, the text extracted from the native PPTX, and an ordered montage of all requested slides. The frozen judge is gpt-5.6-terra, queried at temperature 0 through the evaluation proxy. The judge returns independent five-point scores for Visual Expressiveness (VE), Instruction Following (IF), and Content, together with functional topology graph for eligible content slides and three serious-defect flags for every requested slide. The judge never receives the system identity. The remaining metrics are computed deterministically from the validated response and the generation manifest. First-Pass Success requires successful and valid native artifact from outer attempt 1 with no failed slides. To provide the judge with complete presentation whenever possible, failed slide may be reconstructed for up to three additional attempts; such recovery does not alter its First-Pass Success status. Layout is computed only over slides that are successfully generated and rendered in the evaluated artifact, consistent with Eq. 13. For each such slide, Layout passes when the judge marks severe overlap, severe clipping, and severe out of bounds as false, and the deck-level score is the fraction of these successfully rendered slides that pass all three checks. Slides that remain failed after reconstruction are excluded from the Layout denominator and are instead reflected by the First-Pass Success metric. Topology is emitted only for successfully rendered eligible content slides (2,. . . ,N-1), and its normalized two-iteration Weisfeiler Lehman similarity is converted to Topo-Vendi. Generation cost and latency are summed from the event ledger and outer-attempt status files, while judge cost is logged separately. The following is the original prompt used for the unified evaluation judge. The prompts output template is appended programmatically and validated before recording any metric. Evaluation Prompts You are strict blinded evaluator of one complete presentation. Evaluate only the presentation brief, deterministic evidence, extracted slide text, and ordered slide montage supplied in this request. Do not infer the generating system. Return five independent outputs: Visual Expressiveness (VE), Instruction Following (IF), Content, content-slide topology, and per-slide Layout flags. Visual Expressiveness (VE). VE is an integer from 1 to 5. Judge purpose-built visual communication, information visualization, visual storytelling, visual richness, aesthetics, and requested-style match. Generic boxes, decorative color, repeated stock imagery, and text inside containers do not by themselves count as strong visual expression. Score 1 means visually broken or overwhelmingly text-only; 2 means sparse, generic, repetitive, or weak; 3 means adequate with noticeable limits; 4 means strong, varied, polished, and effective; 5 means exceptional purpose-built visual storytelling throughout. Do not let content correctness inflate VE. Instruction Following (IF). IF is an integer from 1 to 5. Judge only compliance with explicit instructions: topic, target audience, communication goal, success criterion, style brief, language, requested slide count, and other explicit constraints. Use the deterministic generation evidence for slide count and failed pages. Score 1 means the instructions are mostly unmet; 3 means the main request is met with meaningful omissions; 5 means all explicit requirements are satisfied exceptionally well. Do not let visual polish excuse missed instructions. Content. Content is an integer from 1 to 5 and combines content quality with narrative coherence. Judge relevance, specificity, informativeness, clarity, internal consistency, limited redundancy, logical slide-to-slide progression, appropriate emphasis, and whether the ending follows from the preceding material and serves the communication goal. Penalize generic filler, unsupported specificity, obvious factual errors, repetition, and disconnected slides. Score 1 means unusable or incoherent; 3 means adequate but generic, uneven, or weakly organized; 5 means exceptionally informative, clear, and coherent. Do not reward verbosity. Content-slide topology. Analyze exactly the slide numbers listed under ELIGIBLE CONTENT SLIDES. Emit one topology object per eligible slide and no others. Regions may use only the types title, text, visual, chart, and container; size classes may be only small, medium, or large; groupings may be only row, column, overlay, radial, or freeform; and edges may use only left_of, above, adjacent, aligned, overlap, or contains. Capture functional composition, not wording, color, image identity, or decorative detail. IDs WSDM 27, February 1519, 2027, Hong Kong, China Zhou et al. must be unique within slide, and every edge endpoint must reference region ID from that slide. Layout. Emit exactly one object for every requested slide. Mark only serious, visible defects: severe_overlap is an unintended collision that materially obscures content; severe_clipping is materially cutoff content; and severe_out_of_bounds is content visibly extending beyond the canvas. Intentional overlays, text on shapes, and close spacing are not failures. failed red-X placeholder is not itself an overlap, clipping, or out-of-bounds defect; deterministic code handles failed slides separately. Return exactly one JSON object matching OUTPUT JSON TEMPLATE. The topology and layout arrays in the template illustrate object shape only; populate the required slide numbers stated in the request. Do not return Markdown or additional keys.

sections.title: F Future Work
sections.content: Future work will explore two directions. First, the performance of Topology First is currently constrained by the spatial controllability and robustness of existing inpainting models, which may introduce visual drift or imperfect adherence to the grounded structure during synthesis. As inpainting models become more reliable in following masks, geometry, and regional semantics, we expect Topology First to better realize its potential for combining flexible composition with coherent visual integration. Second, given current resource constraints, we leave system-level post-training for future study. Incorporating post-training signals for presentation aesthetics and visual quality may further improve the polish, consistency, and overall visual appeal of generated slides [17].
